Instead, Emma and her companions come with lifeless performances as they tell a story with every single genre trope in the book, including a quiet hero who has been chosen by prophecy, a heavy-handed nature vs. humans/technology theme, a Force-ghost little girl who isn’t actually there, and an amnesiatic character who at one point is stricken with a dose of amnesia so she remembers even less than before.

None of that would be a deal-breaker for me were it not for the fact that the execution of its trope-filled story isn't delivered with the kind of punch that can make up for it. It's on the weaker side with consistently weak dialogue and reveals I saw coming from about 10 miles away. If you’ve played a JRPG in the last twenty years, there’s nothing about this story that hasn’t been done better in numerous other games, and if you’re expecting the quality to be near the level of something like Xenoblade Chronicles, you’re almost certainly going to be disappointed. It’s especially weird just how flat most of the characters are; they rarely show emotion (sometimes with in-universe reasons, not that the justification makes it more interesting to watch). The robotic animations, lifeless eyes, and long silences in between dialogue makes nearly all the scenes between Emma and her found family pretty hard to sit through most of the time. And they do that thing where they show a washed out flashback to something that literally happened less than five minutes ago, which drives me up the wall way more than it probably should.

Its trope-filled story isn't delivered with the kind of punch that can make up for it.

Also, this isn't really a specific pain point, but I feel obligated to mention just how much of the dialogue is taken up by characters talking about food and the eating of it. It'd make sense if it was woven in thematically, but it's not and I’m not sure if the writers were just super hungry when they wrote this or what, but it’s pretty bizarre.

items.title: House of the Dragon Season 3, Episode 7 Recap and Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
There’s a great fundamental issue at the heart of House Targaryen that has too often gone unexamined and underexplained in House of the Dragon, despite its name, and that’s how the dragons work. This show has followed its predecessor’s example in leaning into the human drama of Westeros and away from its more fantastical aspects, but there’s a limit to how well that works, and in this engaging and generally fun episode (unless you’re Emma D’Arcy’s Rhaenyra), they finally get their teeth, and claws, into it.

The question is what, exactly, is the relationship between rider and dragon for House Targaryen and their allies? What are the obligations between rider and beast, if any? How (or how much) do they communicate? Do their feelings affect one another? There have been suggestions, occasionally, that having a dragon may affect one’s temperament (or that one’s temperament may affect one’s chance of bonding with a dragon); there’s a clear implication that losing your dragon is a form of emasculation for Tom Glynn-Carney’s Aegon II and the late Viserys (Paddy Considine). But it’s never been clear if it matters, and how much, beyond prestige in the internal Targaryen pecking order.

This time, however, we get some key hints that there’s more of a link than perhaps we were shown before. The scenes of dragon conflict, as when Rhaenyra finally discovers that her husband Daemon (Matt Smith) has been lying to her to protect his daughter Rhaena (Phoebe Campbell) and flies to confront both along with Addam (Clinton Liberty), suggest an emotional closeness. As the humans shout at one another, their dragons roar and bellow and, occasionally, threaten to flame, and it’s absolutely clear that they’re reflecting something human and vice versa. Later in the episode we see Aegon screaming in sync with his steed Sunfyre, both disfigured and defiant and apparently on the verge of madness, and the impression is confirmed.

The episode also begins with a dream of Helaena (Phia Saban) and in fact heavily features her dreams - or perhaps Dreams, of the prophetic kind. So what does it mean that she sees herself on her dragon, Dreamfyre, shouting “Dracarys!” as an angry mob rushes at them in the Dragonpit? What does it mean that she imagines a quiet life on the farm with her children (it looks like both Jaehaera and a younger boy, presumably the one she’s currently expecting) when an eclipse occurs? Rhaenyra is putting her younger half-sister under pressure to share her Dreams, desperate for reassurance that she is on the right path, but it’s not clear that Helaena has any such comfort to offer.

The question is what, exactly, is the relationship between rider and dragon for House Targaryen and their allies?

Of course, that’s far from the most screwed-up dream this episode. That prize goes to Aemond (Ewan Mitchell), who sees his mother Alicent (Olivia Cooke) arriving at Harrenhal and the two of them tumbling into bed together before realising it was all a dream. And then he wakes up and she has indeed arrived. Awkward! This may not be the dictionary definition of “headfuck” but it should be. Alicent babbles, Aemond is more taciturn, Alys (Gayle Rankin) is rightly suspicious of the newcomer. Aemond shares her wariness to a degree, enough to murder Alicent’s travelling companion (who, to be fair, is there to help assassinate him), but not enough to refuse the poisoned nightcap she offers after the world’s most awkward meet-the-mother-in-law dinner. Alicent creeps out of the castle and into the wind, figuring that the job is done and stricken by it, but Aemond stumbles to Alys at the first stomach pangs so he’ll probably recover.

Meanwhile Rhaenyra is still pulled in every direction and failing to deal with any of her problems, and it creates a vacuum at the seat of her power. Torrhen Manderly (Dan Fogler) is furious that he’s been left to hold the bag for everyone’s money woes – something that is literally his job -- and Mysaria (Sonoya Mizuno) is trying to make herself a conduit to the people and being rejected on all sides. She manages to, ahem, reconnect with Rhaenyra herself by the end of the episode (is that what the kids are calling it these days?), but she’s still caught in-between a regal rock and a common hard place, and that’s a tough situation to be in.

Daemon, too, is looking more woebegone than we have seen him before. He has belatedly realised that his daughter may desperately need him, which by Westeros standards makes him father of the year against almost zero competition, but in trying to protect her he has broken his wife’s heart. And also, he’s almost entirely failed to protect her; he’s just separated her from her dragon and gone home. He’s also increasingly floundering in council, suffering the same myopia as Rhaenyra and failing to look past his personal passions to the big picture.

It’s a mess. The only person laughing – and laughing a lot this time -- is Ormund (James Norton), who’s riding high despite the imminent arrival of the Rivermen outside his hastily built walls and the fact that he’s probably in last place in that aforementioned father of the year competition. He holds Corlys Velaryon (Steve Toussaint) captive, and cuts off his finger as proof of life to attempt to keep the Velaryon men from plugging the policing gap in King’s Landing (an efficient and speedy postal system still appears to be operating between Tumbleton and King’s Landing). He’s also keeping his ward Daeron (Benjamin Evan Ainsworth) and cousin Gwayne (Freddie Fox) in the dark about his plans, to their increasing frustration. And, in the episode’s final big reveal, he’s courting the dragon rider Ulf (Tom Bennett), trying to turn him from Rhaenyra’s service with the promise that he’ll become Lord of (Corlys’) Driftmark fortress, and also that he’ll be free to drink whenever he wants. It’s not clear which is the bigger inducement to the big ol’ lush but it could spell big trouble for Rhaenyra if he turns.

So the tally was six dragons for Rhaenyra (Syrax, Caraxes, Vermithor, Silverwing, Moondancer, Seasmoke) plus one unreliable wannabe ally (Sheepstealer). Then there was one MIA for the Greens (Vhagar) and one out of combat (Dreamfyre). Now there are five for Rhaenyra, two of them perhaps injured; two for the Greens (it looks like Ulf’s Silverwing and the resurgent Sunfyre) and potentially two MIA dragons (Sheepstealer and Vhagar, still) to potentially change that calculus further. It’s all at play going into the Season 3 finale, and it’s still not clear how far these flames could spread.

items.title: Grand Theft Auto – The Legacy Review
items.author: Luke Reilly
items.content:
Over the next few months, I’m going to be taking a look back at each of the core Grand Theft Auto games and replaying them in the lead-up to the arrival of Grand Theft Auto 6. What we’ll be putting together won’t be traditional re-reviews, and they won’t carry IGN’s typical score out of 10, because it really wouldn’t be at all fair to simply pick apart old games published multiple hardware generations ago and make them sweat under the harsher standards of 2026. What we will be doing, however, is re-examining what made each GTA remarkable upon the time of its release, digging into what they achieved and the legacies they established, and rediscovering how much fun each of them remain today. We’ll also be identifying both the parts of the GTA experience that have seen the most evolution and growth, as well as the parts that remain fascinating, commendable, and timelessly impressive. At the end of the project, using GTA’s previously six-star wanted level, you should be able to get an idea of where each of these games roughly sit in my long-term love for this series. First cab off the rank? The original Grand Theft Auto.

When the original Grand Theft Auto arrived towards the end of the 1990s, it was like nothing I’d ever played before, but it somehow also felt like I’d been in training for it most of my life. On the one hand, it was essentially the digitisation of an entire childhood looming over a 2D toy car mat – my diecast collection scattered around me as I simulated countless car chases from above. On the other, it felt instantly familiar to play – like an intuitive yet anti-social distortion of the top-down delights of Codemasters’ Micro Machines. Grand Theft Auto was bold and brash. It was also brutally unforgiving, regularly frustrating, and cumbersome to control. But despite that, I was consistently drawn to it – like a moth to a flamethrower. Nearly 30 years later, I was more than a little curious about how I’d fare playing it all over again, but I’ve found myself with a largely unchanged opinion – continuously stumped by its absolutely unsympathetic difficulty, yet consistently charmed by its wanton silliness, varied vehicles, hilarious sound effects, and trendsetting original soundtrack.

It’s very easy to look back at the original GTA as a product of a different era, and that goes beyond its old school, top-down aesthetic. Its arcade-style approach to progression, which is baked around trying to maximise your overall score for each level while juggling a very limited set of lives, is nothing like the GTA series we’ve known since its complete reinvention at the dawn of the century. There’s no meaningful story here to speak of; just 90-odd seconds of cutscenes where a gallery of criminal stereotypes either pass on their thanks, or issue you direct threats related to putting unwanted things in your butt.

However, GTA was already a product of a different era upon its initial release in European territories in 1997 – and even more so by its North American launch in 1998. The flat sprites of its vehicles and pedestrians give it that 2D-adjacent look, even if people often gloss over that the cities themselves are actually rendered in 3D. But GTA found itself sandwiched between stuff like the debut of Gran Turismo and the arrival of Half-Life, Unreal, and Metal Gear Solid. We’re talking Tekken 3, Thief, and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. What I’m saying is that we knew where the cutting edge was in the late ’90s, and GTA didn’t really feel like it was on it.

The three maps may not be enormous by modern standards, and the selection of weapons is admittedly slim, but GTA was unprecedented in terms of the open-world freedom it allowed.

And yet it still works, and that’s really thanks to the high level of player agency it offers. The three maps may not be enormous by modern standards, and the selection of weapons is admittedly slim, but GTA was unprecedented in terms of the open-world freedom it allowed. It feels unlikely that anyone at developer DMA Design could’ve fully understood just how stealthily innovative GTA would ultimately be, but it nonetheless laid down the bedrock for sandbox action gaming as a whole. Complete tasks as clinically or as chaotically as you choose. Navigate Liberty City, Vice City, and San Andreas however you see fit. Take whatever vehicle you want, and take on objectives in whatever order works for you. Not interested in completing actual missions? GTA is engineered to allow you to ignore them entirely. You can simply steal cars, wreak havoc with pedestrians, and battle law enforcement.

Make no mistake: GTA is a somewhat clunky game to play. This was true in 1997, and even more so now. To be clear, I don’t personally have major problems with the driving. Yes, it suffers a bit from the jerkiness of the camera zooming in and out. Yes, you’ll bump into other cars regularly as they appear on screen too late to avoid. Yes, some cars are too fast for their own good, with the camera unable to zoom out fast enough (or far enough) to avert spearing into high-speed crashes. Yes, motorbikes are pretty pointless, and I spend more time getting back on them after wiping out than I do riding them in the first place.

Broadly, however, I believe the driving is quite fun – and I suspect a lot of that probably stems from my background with Codemasters’ Micro Machines series. For context, the Micro Machines series was one of the most-loved racers of its era – and certainly one of my own favourites as I grew out of rolling around on the floor making engine noises. Its top-down perspective was really the perfect training zone for a game like GTA, and I would suggest that – in the late ’90s – there’s an incredibly strong chance that a player of GTA would’ve had some kind of previous muscle memory from Micro Machines nestled somewhere in their fingertips.

[Micro Machines’] top-down perspective was really the perfect training zone for a game like GTA.

I can appreciate that without that prior experience there are elements of GTA’s driving controls that may be a little hard to hurdle. For instance, when cars are headed down the screen, from top to bottom, the controls remain consistent. That is, stab left, and your car will turn to its left – and immediately head to the of the screen. It’s ultimately a car, so it’s entirely logical that left is always left; it’d be untenable to have the controls flip mid-corner. But this kind of thing is printed into my brain. It’s second nature – if not from Micro Machines, then from an entirely analogue childhood of racing R/C cars and quickly learning everything is mirrored when they’re racing back towards you. However, I can anecdotally report this was initially a bit of a braintwister for some of my kids, so I can see how the controls might seem a little obtuse at first. I feel like they were initially treating the car’s direction like a cursor, rather than the car as a discrete object.

The lack of an in-game map spun them out a little, too. Luckily, I still have actual fold-out paper maps of these cityscapes, which are genuinely essential to complete certain missions (like quickly finding the nearest bomb shop before a strict timer runs out). They proved to be a neat novelty for kids from a generation who’ll never know what it’s like to navigate your way to an unknown location by leafing through a dog-eared street directory that smells like petrol and wet socks. My GTA maps are a little flimsy these days but, considering GTA 6 and future PlayStation games in general won’t even be getting a disc, they’re also a fun if now bittersweet footnote in the story of physical gaming media.

My GTA maps are a little flimsy these days but, considering GTA 6 and future PlayStation games in general won’t even be getting a disc, they’re also a fun if now bittersweet footnote in the story of physical gaming media. 

It’s on foot where GTA falls down and, unsurprisingly, the same things that frustrated me about it in the late ’90s continue to do so today. For context, the tank-like on-foot controls are a side effect of the fact that this was a time before dual analogue controllers became the default. Whether you’re on PC with a keyboard or PlayStation with a controller, all you can do is turn left and right, and move forward or backwards. Don’t think of it like a primitive version of a modern, twin-stick shooter like Hotline Miami – you’re really just a tiny, slow car with legs. The Micro Machines-style controls make less sense on foot, and they’ve definitely dated.

The upshot is combat is harder than a $2 steak. It's tougher to deal with clunky controls when just one hit will kill your character. Body armour pickups are available, but they’ll only protect you from three hits. It’s also incredibly difficult to line up shots from long distances, and not much easier at close quarters. It’s particularly tricky to turn and shoot at pursuing police since, by the time you do manage to pivot 180 degrees, there’s typically only time to get one or two shots off.

The pistol is a mostly useless weapon overall, in this case. The machine gun is far more effective, since you can spray a burst in an arc and get at least one round to hit. The flamethrower is the most trusty option, but you won’t see a great deal of it without resorting to cheats.

I cheated like hell when I played GTA as a teenager, and I’d honestly be surprised if that wasn’t the case for most people of my vintage. The action is a lot more fun with 99 RPGs in your back pocket. Cheats are very much an integral part of GTA’s legacy. While cheats have become depressingly rare over the last several generations, the GTA series – up until GTA 5, at least – remains one of the last bastions of fun, silly, and useful cheats.

While GTA invariably found familiar ways to frustrate me, there is still a pile of things about it that bring a grin to my face in 2026.

I appreciate the variety of cars, and I greatly admire the way they look. Sure, these 2D sprites are typically quite tiny on screen, but each car has been crafted with enough care that they’re not just blobs of pixels that look vaguely like cars. They have terrific depth, and the curves of an off-brand VW Beetle are noticeable and distinctly contrast the flat and angular lines of a boxy American sedan – despite the fact both are simple 2D images.

I also enjoy that the mix changes up between cities. Vice City has more exotic supercars that are unique to its beachside streets. San Andreas is the only place you’ll find the floral-painted Love Wagon. Each city has bespoke cop cars with different liveries and siren layouts. There’s effort to make each place distinct, and the cars are a big part of making that happen. The seeds the studio planted here in this regard would truly germinate in 2004’s GTA: San Andreas, though it’s crazy to think this happened just seven years later.

Moreover, I love the resemblance that many of the cars have to Matchbox cars of the ’80s, to the point where it’s entirely obvious the team were simply turning photos of actual models into in-game sprites, wholesale. Sure, it’s fair enough to argue that GTA’s F40, Diablo, 911, or Viper lookalikes could have been just as easily gleaned from photographs of the real things than toys, but then you spot stuff like the orange-roofed ambulance, which still sports an identical E on top from its equivalent Matchbox model. Hell, GTA’s Flamer has the whole livery from the Chevy they sourced it from – squint real hard and it still says 57 Chevy on the deck lid!

Even more than the cars, I hugely appreciate the soundtrack. So much effort was made to build a series of radio stations filled with credible-sounding music. Credible is actually an understatement considering how many of these tracks are genuine earworms. You could actually put GTA’s PlayStation disc into a standard CD player and simply play the music. This functionality wasn’t actually unique to GTA at the time, but it’s still nifty. Did I do that? Hell yes, I did. I even recorded it onto a cassette so I could play it in my car.

Beyond that, GTA’s completely silly brand of squelching hit-and-runs and over-the-top violence keenly reminded me of how successfully it weaponised controversy as a free marketing tool around the time of its launch. It certainly wasn’t the first game to cause a ruckus for gratuitous vehicular violence. In actual fact, that distinction is owned by an arcade game called Death Race, released way back in 1976, which caused a huge fuss in the mainstream press for allowing players to run over and kill crude-looking pedestrians on screen. But the hullabaloo around GTA was hefty at the time, even in the immediate wake of Carmageddon – which caused a large fuss of its own a few months before GTA’s launch.

[GTA] certainly wasn’t the first game to cause a ruckus for gratuitous vehicular violence.

Now, even back in the late ’90s I did think the reaction was a little overblown. That is, 1996’s Die Hard Trilogy predated GTA by a year, and that featured pedestrians getting left and right – complete with a wiper animation clearing the blood from the screen when driving in first-person. But, yes, there’s no denying the original GTA pushed the envelope in ways not even the modern series would attempt today, whether that’s mowing down a line of Hare Krishnas, blowing up a school bus, or indeed assassinating the ‘High Priest of Babylon’ – who turns out to be none other than the President of the United States himself. GTA’s low-fi aesthetic makes a lot of this stuff feel pretty goofy and harmless here, but certainly at least some of it would be a little too grim to sync with the satirical sensibilities of the modern series.

Like a Stone Age axe, Grand Theft Auto is hard, primitive, and – honestly – more than a little cumbersome. However, like said axe, it’s nonetheless a valuable artefact that maintains an effective edge to it. Fearless but flawed and endearing but unnecessarily difficult, the original Grand Theft Auto may be tricky to wholeheartedly recommend to anyone who didn’t previously play it during its moment back in the late ’90s, but I can’t deny how fascinating it’s been to re-experience its prehistoric brand of open-world freedom in the context of everything that’s come since. It just demands patience, precision, and a paper map by your side.

Luke is a Senior Editor on the IGN reviews team. You can track him down on Bluesky @mrlukereilly to ask him things about stuff.

items.title: Cape Fear Episode 10 Recap and Review – ‘The Executioners’
items.author: Michael Peyton
items.content:
Spoilers below for Episode 10 of . Season 1 is now streaming on Apple TV.

After 10 episodes of , , craziness, reaches its inevitable gonzo climax this week with a jam-packed hour filled with fire, wind, rain, and the entire Bowden family put on trial. The full season of the Apple TV series has swung wildly from incredible melodrama to clumsy wheel-spinning, but this week’s finale — titled “The Executioners,” in a nod to the novel on which the whole Cape Fear universe is based — mainly sees the show stick the landing, even if the denouement is a frustrating ploy for a Season 2 renewal.

When , she was swimming away from Max Cady’s deranged family, having jumped off his sister’s houseboat after uncovering a slew of their buried secrets. After Anna escapes, Max arrives for a big ol’ miscreant family reunion and castigates his father, sister, and maybe-product-of-incest son for letting her get away. Enraged, Max pulls a gun and shoots both Crystal and possible-son Luke in the stomach before pistol-whipping his father and locking him in a cage. Max then proceeds to dump gasoline over the whole boat and set it ablaze, his family trapped inside.

In a show full of shocking moments, it’s great to see Cape Fear up the ante (and body count) so early in the finale. We think we’re building up to a drawn-out series of major revelations, but instead Max Cady just burns everyone alive. It’s a testament to what the show does best: shocking, over-the-top moments that are at once unhinged and vital to the show’s appeal. While I would have appreciated some further explanation of the entire Cady family’s twisted backstory, the quick execution of an entire boatload of pivotal characters grants new, major insight into Max’s depravity and sets the stage for the season’s final confrontation.

After escaping, Anna finds her way to a road and is promptly hit by a car. She pops up and bums a ride back to Savannah while Tom makes bail thanks to his erstwhile paramour Lexi, who still believes he’s an asshole but “just not a murderer.”

At Max’s restaurant opening (yes, he’s still hellbent on this weird little side project), Anna shows up brandishing what initially seems to be a gun but ends up being a Bluetooth speaker. She holds it up, Say Anything style, and plays Nevaeh’s recorded confession (thanks, Natalie) followed by a video clip of Max urging Amy to kill herself from all the way back in Episode 1. Since Max is famous, naturally the press is at the event and hears every word. Enraged, Max chokes Anna before the cops tackle him to the ground and haul him away.

As literal storm clouds gather overhead (there’s a hurricane coming, remember), the entire family reunites at home. Soon, the cops show up to inform them that, surprise, Max overpowered the SINGLE officer they had driving him to prison and is once again on the loose. They literally tell the Bowdens, “Sorry, we fucked up,” before peacing out.

With Savannah under an evacuation warning, Tom convinces Anna to take the kids out of town while he stays behind to kill Max. As they begin to pack up, we’re given what is probably the most hilariously incredble shot of the entire series: Max Cady, who the cops had been searching for but had not been able to find, standing on top of the roof of the Bowden's home, smiling menacingly while a hurricane builds overhead. It’s the perfect encapsulation of the series as a whole: a visually stunning, shocking image that’s both thrilling and laugh-out-loud funny.

Max jumps off the roof and slams into Zack, who was looking out an open window at the exact wrong time, and takes the boy hostage. Max forces Natalie to tie her parents to chairs and then injects Zack with a superdose of the mind-control drug he had given him in Episode 7. Max then proceeds to put Tom and Anna “on trial,” claiming they conspired to send him to prison for “their own personal reasons.” He threatens to have Zack bite off his own tongue (which he promptly starts to do) before Anna spills it all.

Anna confesses that, during Max’s trial, there was a leak that the jury was deadlocked and, because she was terrified of him, Anna forced Max into a plea deal. There was a chance that the jury would have found him innocent but, fearful that Max was Natalie’s biological father, she wanted to put him away. Anna then details how she suspects that Luke is actually his and Crystal’s son. Max claims this couldn’t be possible because Crystal was incapable of having children. (Notice how he never said that it wasn’t possible because he hadn’t slept with his own sister...)

After a violent interlude in which Max has yet another seizure and pleads to his god Shangó for a verdict for Tom and Anna, Anna puts the pieces of the entire, seedy Cady family mystery together: Crystal was not Luke’s mother, but Max’s wife, Melissa, was. Max didn’t kill his wife and son; Crystal killed Melissa out of jealousy and ripped the baby from her, claiming Luke as her own. Max wasn’t responsible for the murders; it was Crystal all along, and Max inadvertently burned his child alive on the houseboat.

It’s a great climactic sequence in which many of the series' myriad loose plot threads are neatly tied up. Although revealed mainly through exposition-heavy dialogue, the scene is miles better than last week’s terrible revelatory phone call between Nevaeh and Max. This one at least quickly answers numerous open questions and propels the action foward.

As Max wails in agony, Natalie manages to escape and shoots Max in the head with a nail gun. Zack comes out of his drug-induced stupor and attacks Max. Anna manages to stab Max in the back before Tom chases him to the backyard and tackles him into the pool in an attempt to drown him. As Natalie yells, “Kill him!” Anna jumps into the pool and calmly steers Tom away from doing just that, telling him it would be better to let the man who’s been maniacally tormenting her family “die in a cage.” As they pull an exhausted and broken Max out of the pool, the Bowdens huddle together as the rain pours down.

It’s an extremely unsatisfying moment in what, to this point, had been a stellar final episode. Not having Max Cady meet his end is an obvious ploy for a Cape Fear Season 2 renewal. After all the Bowdens had been through — all the lost appendages, strangers living in their walls, false incarcerations, jobs lost, and reputations ruined — to think that they would let Max Cady live is borderline laughable. The Bowdens, as the series has shown time and time again, are not good people, and it’s unbelievable to think that they’d let their tormentor see the light of day.

Despite this, “The Executioners” is an entertaining, serviceable finale to an action-packed season of television. Even though it ends with an annoyingly overt nod to a potential continuation (the last shot is Amy Adams’s Anna literally LOOKING OVER HER SHOULDER while her family enjoys a barbecue), the major revelations, shocking character deaths, and tight climax bring a mostly satisfying end to the show.

If there’s one consolation to the frustrating final moments of the episode, it’s that we may one day be graced with more gloriously colorful, mind-bending, and outright insane interactions between the Bowden family and the man who nearly destroyed their lives. It seems impossible, after all they’ve been through, that the Bowdens would interact with Max Cady; if they were smart, they'd pack their bags and immediately get the hell out of town.

But, having watched all 10 episodes of Cape Fear’s first season, we know that if a maniacal, malevolent psychopath somehow waltzes back into their lives in a second season, the Bowdens won’t be able to stay away.

items.title: Star Trek: Strange New Worlds Season 4, Episode 2 Recap and Review - What Horrors Lurk on the USS Griffin?
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
Hey, what do you know? In the latest episode of Strange New Worlds, James T. Kirk (Paul Wesley) is bumming around with the crew of the Enterprise again. But man, did he pick the wrong week to play third wheel to La’an (Christina Chong) and Spock (Ethan Peck). “I can’t shake the feeling I’m in the wrong place,” he says in his log, even if he doesn’t realize how right he is about that statement.

“The Griffin Incident” is a full-on haunted house episode, a horror story set on a Constitution Class starship that has plenty of creepy-crawly moments as well as some big-time gore the likes of which we haven’t seen since Star Trek: Discovery Season 1, when that show was flirting with how far it was willing to push the sex and violence factor in the new-for-the-franchise streaming space. It didn’t take long for Disco to realize Star Trek didn’t need to lean into that stuff too much, but for whatever reason this episode of Strange New Worlds goes back to that well again, even if it doesn’t need to. It’s scary the gore.

Things start with the three officers heading back from the “Future Federation Leaders Retreat” – those kiss-asses – only to come across a good old-fashioned mysterious signal that needs investigating. And that, of course, leads them to the USS Griffin, a long-missing Starfleet ship that they soon find out is chock-full of horrors.

Once aboard, they realize that everything is out of whack. There’s gravity and oxygen even if there shouldn’t be, there’s no sign that anything bad has happened onboard, and yet the computer is fracked and there are no crewmembers to be found… well, aside from the ghost lady who is walking around the ship and seemingly disappearing at will. This leads to a fun exchange between Spock and Kirk:

Spock: “There are faint traces of negatively charged ions.”

Kirk: “You mean a ghost?”

Spock: “I mean negatively charged ions.”

That’s where this episode works best – in the character dynamics that are explored because of the horrors the trio encounter.

And really, that’s where this episode works best – in the character dynamics that are explored because of the horrors the trio encounter. As they begin to split up (this is a horror story after all!), they each encounter strange and horrible illusions that feed into – or are fed by – their subconscious. For Spock it’s the human vs. Vulcan debate, for Kirk it’s the abandonment of his family, and for La’an it’s the burden of her genetically-enhanced origins and the potential changes that were happening to her in regards to that even before she landed on the Griffin.

At times, the episode actually evokes the old Next Generation story “Night Terrors,” right down to the corpse in a body bag coming back-to-life moment that happens while Spock is trapped in sickbay. Bringing T’Pring (Gia Sandhu), or an illusory version of her, back to explore Spock’s anxieties is a nice touch, and it’s comforting hearing her say all the things you’d hope she would say to Spock – telling him she did not care for surprises was a mistake, she has sought therapy since their break-up, she did not love him as he deserved. But of course, this is Dream T’Pring, or rather Nightmare T’Pring, which means that cutting Spock’s ear tips off with scissors is also part of the deal. The lesson he learns from all this? Humanity is his greatest strength.

As for Kirk, the writers of the show continue to back-fill his history with more info on Carol Marcus, and now their son David as well. Kirk feels the gravitational pull of his career versus family life, and the tragic part of this thread is that we also know how this story will end. Despite however many trinkets Kirk brings back for David “like an apology for never being around,” as was the case with Kirk’s father, his relationship with David will wind up being even worse than his and Sam’s is with their dad. He won’t even know his son, and as illusory Sam predicts, “We’re gonna die out here in space alone like Kirks are born to do.” That will eventually happen to both Kirk and David, and La’an later spells out David’s fate even more explicitly: “Your little boy is going to die just like you, at the end of a blade, bleeding out in a dark corner of space.”

Packing in details of Kirk and Spock’s backstories is very delicate work. Knowing where Spock goes in the chronology of things, it kind of feels like the lesson he learns here is coming too early for the character, even if it’s dramatically satisfying in this telling. But the Kirk stuff really works for me; I appreciate learning about this absent father of his (Chris Hemsworth!?) and how it no doubt fed into the man Kirk himself became, and why things wound up the way they did between him and Carol and David. That the episode ends with his unanswered message to Carol and David only drives home that the Kirk series showrunners Henry Alonso Myers and Akiva Goldsman were teeing up (and which surely isn’t happening at this point) could’ve been very interesting.

Over on the La’an side of things, the premise of her losing control of her augment side and giving into her famous ancestor’s conquering ways looks to be an ongoing story this season, and here the mysterious effects onboard the Griffin bring out an ugly aspect to her. She’s already bothered by the realization from last week that something is changing with her (Spock asking her if everything’s alright keys us onto that fact), but as she starts to identify with and/or become possessed by the ghost woman onboard – who turns out to be former Griffin security chief Rose Harper – the Jack Torrance-ing of La’an kicks in. By the time she tries to beam Ortegas (Melissa Navia) (!), and finds herself holding a knife to Uhura, she seems to be completely lost. (No wonder Uhura never talked about her on the old show!) It’s only a last-minute rescue by the Enterprise that saves her and Kirk, who she had put that knife right through.

That the episode ends with La’an seemingly spotting Harper out on the Griffin doing the “shhhh” finger to the mouth thing is kind of frustrating, as is the episode’s unwillingness to answer the question of what really happened on the Griffin. Was it truly haunted, or was it just another outer-space weirdo incident? We’ll likely never know, but clearly La’an’s struggle has only just begun.

Questions and Notes from the Q Continuum:

  • “You know, I never liked her.”
  • Everyone’s heard of the Griffin it seems? I get Starfleet folks knowing about it. But T’Pring too?
  • Kirk was a boy scout after all! Don’t forget, in Wrath of Khan when the adult David refers to Kirk as “that overgrown Boy Scout,” Carol replies, “Jim Kirk was many things, but he was never a Boy Scout.” Of course, we always knew she wasn’t strictly referring to the literal idea of the Scouts with that statement…
  • Maybe it’s just taken me this long to notice this, but the transporter sounds in this episode sure have a “The Cage” vibe to them.
  • What the heck is Division 12 and why have we never heard of it before? Apparently the ghostbusters of Starfleet – or the Mulder and Scully? – they’re mentioned enough in this episode that you’d expect to hear from them again later this season.
  • Hey, Carol just got approved for a dream project. I wonder what that could be!
  • Nightmare Sam pulls a Newborn from Alien: Resurrection. Ouch.
  • Stranglings, stabbings, beamings into open space. Take your pick.

items.title: I Want Your Sex Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
Given his last film was over a decade ago, it’s definitely gratifying to have a unique voice in cinema like Gregg Araki back with a new movie, even if the end result is entertaining but not a top tier new addition to his filmography. The indie director broke out in the 1990s with offbeat, edgy movies like The Doom Generation and Nowhere; he’s certainly never been shy about exploring sexuality in his work, which — as you might expect by the title — is front and center in his new release, I Want Your Sex. Araki has spoken about how a motivating factor for this story, co-written with Karley Sciortino, was the oft-repeated notion of Gen Z generally having less sex and being more prudish than the previous generation, an assertion he examines through the eyes of Gen Z protagonist Elliot (Cooper Hoffman).

Elliot’s life gets thrown into disarray thanks to his new job as an assistant for Erika Tracy (Olivia Wilde), a popular modern artist known for her provocative imagery. The very bold and forthright Erika initiates a sexual relationship with Elliot, which gets very wild very quickly, and all while he begins to have some big problems sticking to her rule of this being only about the sex and nothing else.

The first half of I Want Your Sex is very strong, with Araki’s quirky and sometimes surreal sense of humor shining through in the scenes at Erika’s studio as Elliot bonds with one of his coworkers (Mason Gooding’s Zap) while trying to avoid the wrath of Erika’s business manager, Vikktor (a very funny Daveed Diggs, who gets big laughs through some expert glares). Elliot’s central journey into becoming a submissive boy toy to his beautiful and powerful boss is funny and outrageous, with Araki really nailing the casting with his two leads.

On the heels of directing herself in a career-best performance in The Invite, Wilde is also great here as Erika, who has turned her whole life into a form of performance art. Wilde does a nice job of walking the line to keep us guessing about whether Erika really is as unaffected and amusingly laser focused as she seems, or if it’s really all artifice she’s built up around her. Meanwhile, Hoffman continues to impress early in his career following films like Licorice Pizza and The Long Walk. His incredibly accessible and likable boy next door charm is perfect for Elliot, making the character very endearing as he’s being pulled into Erika’s vortex, saying yes to anything and everything because the sex itself and his glee that she’s chosen him is so euphoric.

It’s a very funny, awkward, outrageous sequence that moves between broad comedy, sexiness, and discomfort in an impressive manner. 

The movie’s standout sequence occurs when Erika tells Elliot she wants to have a threesome and tasks him with quickly finding their third; he impulsively asks his college friend and current roommate, Apple (Chase Sui Wonders), to join them. Wonders, who has impressed on The Studio, is terrific here as we see her character spiral through the excitement and tension of the imminent situation. She’s been fangirling over Erika from afar, but she’s about to cross a line with her friend. It’s a very funny, awkward, outrageous sequence that moves between broad comedy, sexiness, and discomfort in an impressive manner.

That sequence, however, is also kind of where the movie peaks, even though there’s plenty more movie after it. The third act of I Want Your Sex inevitably has to deal with the film’s framing device, as Elliot is being interviewed by two police detectives (Johnny Knoxville and Margaret Cho) in the wake of some sort of dark event. And unfortunately, the revelations here feel a bit slapdash and less engaging than what came before it. (Am I aware of how many sentences in a review of a movie called I Want Your Sex can be seen as a sexual pun even when not intended as such? I am, dear reader…)

A couple of notable aspects about I Want Your Sex’s final act feel off. There’s more than one major line crossed by a character that both the person affected and the movie itself seem to be letting off the hook too easily. One element in particular is oddly not even really brought up again in a significant manner, despite the fact that its importance is something this movie in particular should acknowledge. It’s also annoying how Apple vanishes in the second half! There’s a plot reason for why she’s off-screen, but given her role in the film, it’s odd that we don’t really get any closure on this character after we spent significant time with her.

More so, though, it feels like the early scenes in which Araki directly tackles the guarded way young people might perceive sex these days and why that might be — growing up as part of the COVID generation is evoked — as well as acknowledging the power imbalance between Erika and Elliot are subjects that are pushed aside by the end. The movie veers into seeing this as more of a wild May/December relationship, glossing over the other interesting issues it was initially weaving in.

items.title: Tony Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
will be released in select theaters on August 7 before expanding nationwide on August 21.

Eschewing the birth-to-death structure of celebrity biopics — as well as estate-mandated aggrandizing — Matt Johnson’s Tony focuses on a few chapters in the life of Anthony Bourdain from his 2000 memoir, Kitchen Confidential: Adventures in the Culinary Underbelly. During a summer spent in Cape Cod in the mid-1970s, teenage Tony learns for the first time that food, travel, and culture might be his forté. However, the late chef is hardly painted with a hagiographic brush; in fact, actor Dominic Sessa () builds on minor details from the book, like Bourdain’s cocky swagger and the ridiculous nunchucks he kept tucked into his belt, to create an insolent, selfish, but ultimately driven version of a man whose name we’d come to know.

The movie is a blast, ensuring that Johnson is two-for-two this year alongside his time travel mockumentary,Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie; however, the two films could not be more different in scope and style. If anything, Tony — a more measured and intentional work — shares its tonal DNA with Johnson’s, an intense tale of innovators and eventual failures, which grew out of the post- tech biopic boom. It also wouldn’t be a stretch to call Tony one of the only films to truly understand and recreate what made The Social Network tick: the energy of naïve youth, no matter how destructive.

Part dramatic biography, part coming-of-age comedy, and wholly exciting, Tony begins with a highly fictionalized chapter in Bourdain’s life that sees him fibbing about a writing fellowship at Vassar so he can follow his high school crush, Nancy (Emilia Jones), to Cape Cod. The self-proclaimed author has dreams of grandeur and waxes poetic to anyone who’ll listen (drunkenly, might I add), even if it gets him in hot water. The next thing he knows, he’s working as a dishwasher in a local clam joint to make ends meet while keeping this lowly job a secret from his college peers, and sleeping on the porch hammock of his unnamed Portuguese boss, known only as “Chef” (Antonio Banderas).

The plot follows the growing proximity between Tony and Nancy in the perpetual dusk of Provincetown, but it also sees the young teen learning about the adult world — not only through his boss’ passions and failures, but through the drug-fueled sexual exploits of his coworker, Sal (Leo Woodall). Every male role model in Tony’s life seems to harbor a mysterious melancholy, leading to a fascinating set of performances from the cast. Woodall hides an aggrieved sadness just behind his eyes, while Banderas appears to live with regrets he’s long come to terms with. However, these are mere clues that inform each casual interaction rather than eclipsing the central drama. Ultimately, the mile-a-minute bustle of the cramped kitchen is where the movie lives and breathes, from the uncouth rituals of other supporting players (one particularly verbose cook is played by comedian Stavros Halkias) to the slow transition of Bourdain’s own POV on his new lot in life.

The film adapts only two short initial chapters of Kitchen Confidential, so apart from the broad details of time and place, it may as well be fiction. However, Johnson imbues the story with the spirit of Bourdain himself, capturing not only the tone of his writing (snappy, yet colorful), but the gradual widening of his perspective to consider food as a passion, an art form, and a series of local traditions. Most importantly, it reconnects artistry and artist as broad concepts, refusing to divorce creativity from even the most selfish emotional impulses. If The Social Network reframed Facebook as a romantic wound made manifest in isolation, Tony treats Bourdain’s culinary explorations as stemming from romantic pursuit while surrounded by community.

If the movie drops the ball in one notable way, it’s that Nancy is never quite fleshed out beyond this function in the story, making for some awkward (and at times retrograde) “get the girl” framing. However, Tony also unfolds through the perspective of a hot-blooded teenage boy, and includes all the things a lanky ne’er-do-well like Sessa’s Bourdain might find fascinating or alluring. It moves at the speed of rose-tinted thought, with careful visual compositions that get the point across instantaneously so they can be edited together with controlled chaos. All the while, Sessa makes for a fascinating centerpiece as a young man in search of himself, but with no way to find the right questions, let alone the answers, until he hurts those around him and learns from his mistakes.

Tony moves at the speed of rose-tinted thought.

It’s a feel-good guy movie in the vein of Richard Linklater’s, another college period piece that similarly gazes backward in time while immersing you in its testosterone-drenched escapades, but with enough intellectual distance to excuse its visceral delights as a matter of nostalgic retrospective. It grants permission, in a way, to return to a time when the world seemed so large that anything could be possible, even when the weight of expectations bore down on you with unrelenting force.

It’s perhaps no coincidence that as much as Sessa channels the spirit of Bourdain, he also resembles Johnson himself in look and fast-talking demeanor. This ensures that Tony’s exploration of creative spark as something impure but no less valuable feels deeply personal too, as though the film were about eking out a daring space for filmmaking in the Canadian landscape in the way that Johnson and his cohorts often have. Either way, the result is a biopic laser-focused on the follies of youth and hyper-charged with all its vigor.

items.title: The Relic: First Guardian Review
items.author: Michael Higham
items.content:
From a distance, The Relic: First Guardian looks like it could be a solid addition to the growing ranks of B-list action games that punch above their weight. The sort of recommendation you drop your friends who are looking for something to scratch that itch between big games to let them know you’re into this action-game lifestyle, for real. Upclose, The Relic is the exact opposite. It’s clearly inspired by bigger games within and around the FromSoftware lineage, but doesn’t even come close to meeting the high bars they set. It doesn’t even execute its own goals well – shoddy and broken throughout, barely propped up by its engaging combat and let down by how lackluster or straight up unacceptable every other piece of it is.

Visually, The Relic does not make a good first impression nor does it make a great impression at any point afterward. Most character models are bland, either run-of-the-mill medieval European fantasy peasants, knights, and preachers; or designs bizarre enough to be curious but feeling incomplete like your Bloodborne Doll stand-in, Elisa. Faces, and especially your protagonist's mug, seem to have no actual detail on them, short of eyes that glow sometimes. And they all have a sort of low-res fuzz surrounding them akin to the infamous bloom effect from the old Fable games.

The lands you explore have the mood of a dead world with how most of its settlements are ghost towns and all of its fortresses are ruins, and yet they all look nearly identical from one crumbling building to another. The few towns that do still have people in them feel almost indistinguishable from one another. The mix of geography and whatever hazy color filter is fogging everything up is the biggest indicator of which of the three main regions you’re in. The Faded Mist Forest is a dense hinterland with a minty green tint. Hillsbrad has that yellow glow like American movies in the 2010s set in foreign countries, lathered over its rolling hills while a vomit emoji green tint covers its swamps. These color filters get oppressive in burning villages, where everything has an orangey red glow that makes details like pathways to progress hard to find and the overall image quality look smudged. Then you have caves that artificially narrow your field of view by darkening the edges of the screen, really testing your peripheral vision.

I did find exploring the regions to be occasionally intriguing, so long as I could avoid getting stuck on random geometry or loading waist deep into the ground at a checkpoint. There is genuine intrigue in finding a promising cave mouth or walking up a flight of stairs into a mysterious tower, which would only lead an elevator to bring you back down from the top. But sometimes it results in time spent trying to understand how a fast travel point ended up completely embedded inside a wall to be inaccessible and completely useless. It’s very easy to get pulled away from main paths and into side quests or dungeons around the corner because records left behind by lost or fallen characters. These dot the countryside, leading you into points of interest like a breadcrumb trail. These often reveal stories of loss told by your character making Batman-like deductions based on some sort of noteworthy thing in the environment like a broken cart, or told in the voice of the characters involved who conveniently left progressively revealing notes behind right before their demise. Seriously, I know every game does a version of this kind of storytelling, but The Relic really abuses this particular storytelling technique with a frequency and reckless abandon I don’t think I've seen before.

[It's] shoddy and broken throughout, barely propped up by its engaging combat.

Many of these side stories, based on Korean folklore, are somewhat compelling, even moving at times. A memorable one involved a woman running out to the forest to find her husband who hadn’t returned home with the other soldiers from a battle. When you retrace her steps, you find that her grief had turned her into a monster (an admittedly common trope The Relic leans on to punctuate these stories with boss fights). They don’t all end with a bang, though. One story had me trek up a mountain reading scraps of notes from a wife waiting for her husband to return as their daughter gets more and more anxious, playing with pinwheels to pass the time. At the top of the climb was just a grassy plateau, filled almost hauntingly with pinwheels presumably left there by a daughter who eventually stopped waiting. I liked the rare occasions when a story resolved in a subversive way, and was disappointed when these kinds of stories had boss fights wedged into them awkwardly.

The side stories and dungeon bosses are the best way to get loot of any meaningful value in The Relic. The rolling hills, deep forests, and dank dungeons of its world have hundreds of shiny little loot markers scattered into every nook and cranny, and almost all of them are just a scant pile of 30 to 50 gold. You’ll sometimes find chests guarded by bad guys or tucked at the end of a divergent path in a cave, and almost all of them have about 600 gold. If you’re thinking, “That's weirdly specific,” well, so did I for about 20 hours until I stopped touching any of those all together since I was already carrying more gold than I could responsibly spend by the third act. As someone who genuinely enjoys clearing activities and map markers in games, my 30-or-so hours with The Relic is the first time I can remember being turned off at the idea of getting loot all together.

That said, many of these stories are often overwritten and put together in a strange way that suggests it was essentially put through translation software without any other linguistic touch or localization effort. This goes for most dialogue as well; whenever I think a shopkeeper or guard whose conversation I’m eavesdropping on is done, more lines of dialogue keep pouring out clumsily. The text in the captions also regularly don’t match what you hear coming from voice lines, and this is made even worse by the generally poor voice performances across the board – I almost couldn’t believe that some of the takes I heard made it into the final game.

Fighting the looters and monsters that roam the land is where The Relic is at its most cohesive, but thats a relatively low bar that it barely clears. Each of the five available weapons are distinct from one another; while each one only has one combo string, you can’t just mash it out since each subsequent swing requires the proper timing. The sluggish responsiveness from the controls make this rhythm a chore to lock down in the early game, and I found myself dropping strings that felt right even after some practice. Only your defensive options cost stamina, encouraging you to be aggressive more freely – however, enemies rarely stagger or flinch from attacks , so you’ll spend plenty of time waiting for openings anyway. Like you, enemies can be stunned when they’ve run out of stamina through either your attacks or when you parry theirs, but it’s frustrating that they don’t have visible stamina bars so you’ll never know how close they are to a full stagger until it happens.

Each of the three regions (with the second being split into two subregions) have their own roster of key bad guys specific to them, but none of the regular fodder test your skills all that regularly on their own. In packs, they can present moments where you need to think tactically to minimize harm – archers hiding behind a double-wide brute with an axe become priority targets for your own self-recharging elemental spell bolt, for example. Groups of monsters are the most dangerous when they join the fray, due in part to the janky lock-on system and jittery camera becoming woefully unreliable. Foes can trap you and wear you down partially because you can't switch between targets fast enough or get a read on what’s going on, but that doesn’t necessarily negate actual interesting encounter design.

With the exception of a few standouts like a weird cultist who holds a brazier on his head or some unfortunate cave dwellers with mining equipment for heads, enemies don’t have the visual appeal worthy of a top tier grimdark fantasy world. They feel like they’re trying to be like some other creatures in a FromSoftware game or ape the twisted nature of that aesthetic. After a while, they just become annoyances, neither valuable for farming materials since they only drop middling amounts of gold, only good for buying basic items or low-level crafting items that I could just go buy somewhere. By the late game, I would do my best to completely avoid them out in the world, running past them to the next checkpoint while in dungeons as I ran out of patience for their nonsense.

Bosses have a bit more going for them in both these respects, as their attacks create way more of a puzzle to solve and generally look more detailed and more interesting then run of the mill mooks. But these fights are also where I had to employ the most tedious tactics in order to avoid the cheapest deaths. There are a lot of bosses – over 75 to be clear, and most of them are optional. The worst of these take advantage of The Relic’s aforementioned technical woes while also having to contend with environmental hazards, status effects they cheese on you, or relentless offense that you can’t reliably interrupt. A handful of these fights also just break completely in weird ways. For example, the boss just stopped moving completely in one of these fights, awed by my desperate dodge rolling, I’m sure. In another, the boss would sometimes just not show up at all when I respawned, leaving me in an empty room that they could occasionally fire into, which I couldn't leave without reloading my entire session.

As a consolation, weapon skills really spice up combat, adding some punchy offensive and defensive options into the mix. The more skills you unlock for each weapon, the more complete they feel with a more fleshed out moveset, and each weapon has a two-sided skill tree that firmly divides them into even more distinct playstyles. The battle staff is a good example of this, with one side making you a dangerous whirlwind in melee and the other giving you some very powerful ranged options that almost fills the role of a traditional mage. However, the massive amount of relic points required to unlock all these skills on any one path will make it hard to see the full scope of a style before very late game. You can’t grind these points either, as they only come as either rewards from certain boss fights or some quests, or can be found at specific blue shrines out in the world. With an item that is really easy to come by, you can refund any points invested and respec as you see fit. I did this many times in order to try out or switch between different playstyles if I thought a new approach was needed to get through a new boss.

Everything about this experience, including its combat, is marred in some way by its own shambolic state.

Equipment have passive abilities and drawbacks, some of which have pronounced effects on combat. One of the two-handed weapons lowers the stamina cost of blocking while raising the cost to dodge. A battle staff has a small chance of replenishing all of your cooldowns when you connect with a skill. Relics are stones that modify or enhance your stats, and add an extra layer of customization. With some outside the box thinking, these can bring flair to your builds, which worked well enough to where I didn’t care much that there is no regular stat progression or leveling up at all. Most relics are basic, raising hit points or stamina, bolstering defenses, and so on, but some can offer some unique features like temporary invincibility when you take fatal damage. There's a pair of relics that interact with special attacks that seem like they would be a cool combo, but like most of the sloppy design in The Relic, it didn’t explain which special attacks they applied to or even what special attacks are at all.

items.title: Blacklyte Atlas Lite Standing Desk Review
items.author: Bo Moore
items.content:
We all know by now that even if you have a great chair, sitting for too long brings a myriad of musculoskeletal and metabolic risks. That's why standing desks, which can move to almost anywhere within their range to accommodate the most ergonomic positioning, are such game changers. The problem with a good standing desk, however, is usually its price. Enter Blacklyte and its Atlas Lite Standing Desk. As the "Lite" in the name suggests, it has fewer frills than other standing desks, including the company's own Atlas, but at half the price, you're giving up surprisingly little from a practical standpoint.

Blacklyte Atlas Lite – Options, Assembly, and Setup

The Atlas Lite Standing Desk is available in Obsidian Black, Moonstone White, and Natural Oak colorways. The Obsidian Black is the same color throughout, while the Moonstone White retains the black control panel. The Natural Oak is identical to the Moonstone White, except it features a Natural Oak-colored desktop.

The Obsidian Black is available in Small (47.2 inch width), Medium (55.1 inch width), and Large (63 inch width) sizes. The Moonstone White and Natural Oak are available in Medium, Large, and Extra Large (70.9 inch width) sizes. Small and Medium desktops can handle up to 220 lbs of distributed weight, while Large and Extra Large can handle up to 265 lbs.

All four desktop sizes feature a depth of 31.5 inches, which is on the generous side in comparison to other desks, standing or otherwise. This extra room can easily accommodate large or multiple monitors, allowing you to stand or sit back at a more comfortable distance.

I received the Obsidian Black in Medium, which came in two boxes. The desktop box weighed a beefy 73.6 lbs, with the desktop itself coming in at around 60.2 lbs. The box with the two legs came in at 50 lbs, with the legs themselves roughly 46.3 lbs, thanks to each one having its own motor.

It's not a difficult build, but it definitely requires two people because of all that weight. For the step that involved attaching the feet to the legs, I found that having a third person helped with alignment. In any case, you mostly use the included Allen key to secure the screws, building the legs first, then attaching them to the desktop.

There's a wire cover for the center underside crossbar, which is used to run the cables from the legs to the control panel. The control panel, which can be placed on the far right or far left of the desktop, is attached with different screws using the included Phillips screwdriver. The same screwdriver is then used to attach a cable management box to the rear of the desktop. Finally, the AC adapter is plugged into the control panel and then into the wall.

Blacklyte Atlas Lite – Form and Functionality

The recycled woodfibre desktop material has a nice glossy melamine laminate finish and rounded corners. Save for the flashy Blacklyte logo on the lower left corner of the desktop, it's an elegant design. As expected for a glossy surface, however, it does pick up a lot of fingerprints, so be sure to have a good microfiber cloth on call.

A metal frame runs along the perimeter of the underside of the desktop. This is great for stability, but does create a 2.3 inch thick surface, which can limit what you attach. I found work best, but even then, you have to make sure they can open up enough to fit. There's also a centered indent at the back of the desktop that's great for routing cables behind, particularly in conjunction with the cable tray that's directly underneath.

The plastic control panel is a bit flimsy and basic, but it has all of the functionality you need. Besides the up and down buttons, there are four memory presets, which are set at the current position by holding the number down until it beeps. Thanks to the dual motors, you don't have to wait long for the desk to quietly rise or lower. It only takes about 16 seconds to go from its lowest possible height of 27.5 inches to its highest of 46 inches. While more expensive standing desks may go a bit faster and better accommodate individuals taller than 6 feet 2 inches, for most needs, this should be plenty. However, if you're 6 feet 4 inches or taller, definitely look for a standing desk that can go to 48 inches or higher for better ergonomics.

The desk is reasonably solid thanks to the weight and metal frame, although there's some shake when not at a lower, seated height. A stability crossbar between the two legs would have probably helped provide that last bit of extra shake resistance, but its omission does keep the under-desk area far more usable.

Speaking of stability, I have a love/hate relationship with monitor arms. I love the concept, but have rarely found a monitor arm that remains reasonably stable, yet versatile. Fortunately, the optional Atlas Monitor Arm ($149, but like the desk, often on sale) is more in the love category. It's well-built overall and extremely adjustable.

The Atlas Monitor Arm simply clamp mounts in the area behind the desk that has a slight indent. I had no issue attaching it to a 34 inch LG Ultrawide Monitor. One disappointment was that one of the plastic cable clips arrived broken, so that's one thing the company can definitely improve. Otherwise, it's a great first party accessory.

While the Atlas Lite Standing Desk lacks the lighting, magnetic surface, and some of the other features found in the standard Atlas, it's hard to say that most of those are really necessary. Blacklyte made pretty good calls in regards to the essentials when getting the price down to where it is.

items.title: X-Men '97 Season 2, Episode 7 Review & Recap: "Strange Land, Savage Heart"
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
Warning: This article contains full spoilers for X-Men '97 Season 2, Episode 7!

As strong as the response has been to X-Men '97 so far, I think a lot of X-fans have been pretty impatient for the series to get to Colossus. This is a character who never fully received his due in the original series, and if Nightcrawler can enjoy increased time in the spotlight, why not Piotr Rasputin? Those fans are likely to be thrilled by "Strange Land, Savage Heart," an episode that masterfully explores the compassion that defines both Colossus (Robert Cait) and Nightcrawler (Adrian Hough).

Episode 7 opens by showing us what Colossus and his sister Illyana (Courtenay Taylor) were up to on the day Genosha died. I'll grant that it's pretty disappointing to see a character with as much unexplored potential as Illyana killed off so abruptly, though my hope is that the series can still use her death as an excuse to get into the Limbo of it all eventually. For now, though, her death becomes a logical catalyst for Colossus to do exactly what he did back in the '90s comics - turn his back on Xavier's dream and throw his lot in with the Acolytes.

From there, Episode 7 establishes a new conflict to test the fledgling X-Corp team. Exodus (Bo Poraj) and his Acolytes have kidnapped noted scumbag bigot Graydon Creed (Ben Pronsky), forcing our heroes into action to stop Creed's assassination. The series continues to make the most of the complicated political climate it's established, with this episode really demonstrating the value of having X-Corp operating alongside the more traditional, school-focused X-Men. I only wish Season 2 had a few more episodes, so we could continue seeing the two teams carrying out missions and dealing with this chaotic new reality. But with two chapters left in Season 2, I suspect it's all Apocalypse from here on out.

Episode 7 could have given us a straightforward conflict between X-Corp and the Acolytes, but I'm glad that's not quite the path it chooses. We've already seen the X-Men outnumbered and fighting for their lives in the Savage Land. Instead, this showdown takes a more philosophical and ideological slant, one that befits a storyline with Nightcrawler and Colossus at the helm. This is a war of words more than it is of fists and energy blasts. Though we do still get a little jungle action courtesy of Bishop (Isaac-Robinson Smith) and Polaris (Carolina Ravassa), a duo who are quickly developing into a very entertaining pair.

The trial sequence is handled nicely, with both Exodus and Nightcrawler making a strong case for their respective points of view. The outcome is also well done, with Exodus jumping the gun to execute Creed and viewers only learning later that, no, Nightcrawler did not successfully appeal to Colossus' sense of mercy. The series may have little interest in Illyana right now, but it definitely makes the most of Colossus here. That's why it's so exciting to see the steel-skinned mutant joining up with the Xavier Insititute at the end. I look forward to seeing this series dig into the threeway friendship between Colossus, Nightcrawler, and Wolverine.

Finally, this episode ends with another tease of what's to come in the final two chapters of Season 2, as X-Force encounters the desicated remains of Apocalypse in Greece. That raises some intriguing new questions for the final conflict. Is Gambit a mere Horseman, or has he become the new host for Apocalypse himself? With the next episode being called "The Dead Man's Hand," I doubt we have long to wait before finding out.

items.title: Batman: Caped Crusader Season 2 Review - Darker, Deadlier, but Still Flawed
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
This is a spoiler-free review of Batman: Caped Crusader Season 2. All 10 episodes of Season 2 will premiere on Prime Video on Friday, July 31.

Batman: Caped Crusader may be the latest in a long lineage of Batman-themed animated series, but its appeal has always been crystal clear. It’s a project that not only brings Batman: The Animated Series co-creator Bruce Timm back to the forefront, but one that allows Timm to work wholly unencumbered by the technological and content limitations that hindered the original BTAS. This is an adult-oriented show that fully leans into the violence, sex, and film noir roots of the Batman franchise. The results continue to be well worth a watch in Season 2, even if the series tends to settle for being different from BTAS more than actually trying to be the superior product.

Season 2 moves forward from its predecessor’s Harvey Dent-focused storyline as Batman (Hamish Linklater) confronts an even more ominous era in Gotham City. The fight to take down resilient crime boss Rupert Thorne (Cedric Yarbrough) is further complicated by the emergence of new Gotham City power players like Riddler (Ronan Raftery) and the enigmatic Joker (Matthew Needham). More than ever, the Dark Knight needs a few good friends by his side, something he’s still learning to accept in Season 2.

The thing about Caped Crusader is that it’s strangely disinterested in Batman himself. That’s a criticism that’s often been overblown when leveled against the various live-action films, but here it certainly holds water. Compared to the many villains and supporting characters on display in the series, Bruce Wayne and his alter ego come across as bland and almost psychologically inert. For a guy who gets his kicks dressing as a bat every night, that’s certainly a choice on the part of Timm and the writers. It’s an issue that is only compounded in Season 2, which keeps Bruce at an even further remove because he’s no longer being psychoanalyzed on Harley Quinn’s (Jamie Chung) couch. Thanks mostly to Linklater’s solid vocal performance, the series is great about drawing a distinction between billionaire playboy and grim vigilante, but it very rarely cuts to the genuine person who exists at the intersection of those two personas. Only Episode 3 strives for something deeper with Bruce.

Ultimately, though, that’s only a significant problem when you don’t consider the utter glut of Batman media on the market. If a more complex psychological portrait of the Dark Knight is what you’re after, there are other, better avenues to explore. Caped Crusader is very clearly more interested in delving into the psychology of the Bat rogues and the supporting cast.

There, Season 2 is largely much more successful. The series places a real premium on allowing viewers to understand and empathize with many of these characters, whether it’s crusading defense attorney Barbara Gordon (Krystal Joy Brown), the righteously vengeful inventor Roxy Rocket (Wunmi Mosaku), or the mentally unstable Rose Canton (Fryda Wolff). I’m perhaps most impressed with the show’s continued handling of Detective Flass (Gary Anthony Williams), a character who’s elevated from one-note bad cop in the comics to a genuinely intriguing figure. Batman himself may be an implacable presence in the series, but so many of these characters exist as complex mirrors of his psyche.

One also has to credit Timm and company for not simply replaying the hits from BTAS when it comes to the antagonist characters. Nearly every villain feels fundamentally different in terms of appearance and background. At times, these characters come across as different for the sake of being different. Take someone like Hattie Tetch (Laraine Newman), a gender-bent version of Mad Hatter who’s so far removed from the source material she might as well be an original character. But for every Hattie, there are several iconic villains who receive major and enjoyable overhauls in Season 2. And there are some returning favorites, for good measure. Chung’s Harley Quinn is once again central to one of the best episodes of the season.

But what of Riddler and Joker, the two characters who form the twin backbones of Season 2’s serialized narrative? Suffice it to say, Caped Crusader finds far more success with one than the other. Like Hattie, Eddie Nygma is distorted to the point of being almost unrecognizable. His love of puzzles and mind games is seriously downplayed. Instead, the show depicts him as a raving psychopath who “riddles” his victim with bullets. None of the fascinating intellectual rivalry between Batman and Riddler is on display here, eliminating the entire point of the latter character in the process.

But Joker is another matter entirely. The show takes its sweet time putting this character into the spotlight (as you’d expect), but once it does, Season 2 really hits its groove. As evidenced by the villain’s dour, shadowy appearance, this is a version of Joker almost wholly inspired by the early Golden Age comics and actor Conrad Veidt’s character Gwynplaine in 1928’s The Man Who Laughs. He’s not a preening trickster or comedian, but a brooding terrorist who holds Gotham entirely in thrall.

Unlike Riddler, Joker never feels different for the sake of being different. He’s simply drawing from a slightly different well than we normally see in Batman media. The character also benefits from an excellent performance by Needham, who brings just the right sort of quiet yet zealous attitude the role demands. He may spend much of the season staring ominously from the shadows, but Joker’s belated presence helps elevate the final few chapters of the season in a major way.

Visually and musically, Caped Crusader still exists in the shadow of its parent series. It makes the most of Timm’s iconic aesthetic, and generally beats out the animation quality seen in DC’s various direct-to-video films, but there are flaws to be found. The series is almost too clean at times. The figures lack the same grimy texture that permeates the environments, and many of the CG-animated vehicles look a bit odd in motion. And while Frederik Wiedmann’s moody orchestral score does its job nicely enough, never does it reach the heights of Shirley Walker’s work on BTAS. That’s sort of the common theme with Caped Crusader. It’s a different and more intensely noir-flavored answer to Batman: The Animated Series, but not necessarily superior.

items.title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
Tom Holland’s run as Spider-Man has been nothing if not consistent. Three solo MCU outings and three supporting appearances leading up to and including Avengers: Endgame have shown Marvel Studios and the Russo Brothers struck gold in casting Holland back in Captain America: Civil War, identifying a guy who has scant few detractors out there thanks to how well he’s able to embody both Peter Parker and Spider-Man. Peter’s struggle to find balance between those poles, as it so often does with Spidey, proves to be the main thrust of Spider-Man: Brand New Day. After Shang-Chi and Wonder Man, director Destin Daniel Cretton scores a hat trick by keeping the next chapter of Peter’s journey a lot more restrained than his latter, cosmically-charged outings, even with telepathic threats and organic web fluid oozing from his wrists in play.

Right out of the gate, it must be said that, as Spidey’s first MCU movie set almost entirely within Manhattan: it’s real good to have New York City so front and center in Brand New Day’s action. It’s part of a more-focused mission statement for the movie that Cretton makes immediately in the opening montage, a swing-and-punch medley which covers the last few years of Peter’s lonely life in a world that has completely forgotten who he is thanks to Doctor Strange’s spell at the end of No Way Home.

With no personal life to cultivate, Peter has been laser-focused on cleaning up the city, and his success has gained him the trust of Detective DeWolff (Liza Colón-Zayas) and the rest of the NYPD, leading to enough operational latitude to drive crime in New York to an all-time low. That progress comes at the cost of Peter forgoing all connection, but a chance spotting of Ned (Jacob Batalon) convinces him to attend a party to see whether that spark between him and not just Ned, but MJ (Zendaya) still lingers somewhere in their subconsciouses. The unexpected emotional turbulence that comes with that is what triggers the physiological changes which threaten to subsume the Peter we all know and love, which manifest as supercharged versions of his existing powers, as well as brand new ones like organic web-shooters.
